title: First quotient factor isomorphism over an isomorphism locus
statement: Let $i:S\prime\to S$ be a homomorphism of commutative rings, $J\prime\subseteq S\prime$, and $J=i(J\prime)S$. Let $f:S\prime/J\prime\to S/J$ satisfy $f(\overline b)=\overline{i(b)}$ and let $e:S/J\cong D_1\times D_2$ be a ring isomorphism. Suppose $c\in S\prime/J\prime$ is idempotent and $f(c)=e^{-1}(1,0)$. Let $U\subseteq\operatorname{Spec}(S\prime)$ be open [def-weil-affine-spectrum], suppose the scheme map over $U$ is an isomorphism [def-weil-locally-ringed-space-morphism], and suppose the image of $D(c)\subseteq\operatorname{Spec}(S\prime/J\prime)$ is contained in $U$. Then there are rings $D\prime_1,D\prime_2$, a ring isomorphism $e\prime:S\prime/J\prime\cong D\prime_1\times D\prime_2$, a ring isomorphism $g:D\prime_1\cong D_1$, and a ring homomorphism $h:D\prime_2\to D_2$, with $e\prime(c)=(1,0)$ and $e(f(r))=(g(e\prime(r)_1),h(e\prime(r)_2))$ for every $r$.

source.place: Proof of Stacks Tag 09XH, original node lines 2529-2541; verified at https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09XH (image openness and final product/localization paragraphs).

proof.text: Construct the product by the elementary Chinese remainder identity for an idempotent: R prime is the product of its quotients by (1-c) and (c). The map is r to its two residue classes and its inverse sends (x,y) to cx+(1-c)y, independent of representatives. This sends c to (1,0). Since f(c)=e^{-1}(1,0), f kills (1-c) in the first projection and (c) in the second, so it induces both factor maps. This is also Mathlib AlgEquiv.prodQuotientOfIsIdempotentElem, Tag 00EM.

Choose t lifting c. The first-factor quotient S prime -> D prime 1 has kernel K prime = J prime+(1-t), with V(K prime) equal to the quotient spectrum image of D(c), hence contained in U. Write Spec(S prime) minus U = V(L). Disjointness implies L+K prime=S prime. Choose 1=l+k, l in L, k in K prime, and set g=t*l. Because t(1-t) belongs to J prime, g-t=-tk belongs to J prime. As g belongs to L, D(g) is contained in U.

Restriction of the scheme isomorphism to D(g) identifies the section rings, which are S prime localized at g and S localized at i(g). The induced section map agrees with i on global sections, so it is the canonical localization map.

The two first-factor kernels are K prime=J prime+(1-g) and K=J+(1-i(g)); the second follows from f(c)=e^{-1}(1,0). Since J=map i J prime, K=map i K prime. The localization isomorphism carries their extended ideals to each other, hence induces an isomorphism of the localization quotients. As g and i(g) become 1, these localization quotients are the original first-factor quotients S prime/K prime and S/K. The resulting isomorphism is precisely the induced first-factor map. Combine it with the second-factor homomorphism.
